coverageDimensions:
SERVICE coverage would mean: which AWS services can Amazon Inspector scan with these collectors — ECR, EC2, Lambda, and so on. THIS PAGE GIVES YOU NOTHING. It names no AWS service as a scan target. Amazon Q Developer and Kiro CLI do appear on the page, but as third-party-style applications being scanned, not as services being covered — reading them as AWS service coverage would be a category error.

REGION coverage would mean: in which AWS Regions this ecosystem collection is available. THIS PAGE GIVES YOU NOTHING. It names no Region, no Region table, no "available in all Regions where Amazon Inspector is available" sentence. That is coherent — Sbomgen is a downloadable binary you run on a host or in a build, so much of it has no Regional dimension at all. If you need Region coverage for Amazon Inspector, it is on other pages, not this one.

RESOURCE TYPE coverage would mean: which AWS resource types (ARN-bearing things like AWS::ECR::Repository or AWS::EC2::Instance) this reaches. THIS PAGE GIVES YOU NOTHING USABLE. The closest it comes is naming scan targets in passing — "container and localhost scans" in the intro, and "container, directory, and archive scans" in the AI agent skills section — which is a scan-target axis, not an AWS resource type axis, and it is dropped in prose rather than enumerated as a supported list. Do not build a resource-type claim from it.

What this page DOES give you is a fourth dimension that the three standard ones miss entirely: third-party software application coverage (79 applications across 39 vendor/ecosystem groupings), with per-collector operating system as a real second dimension (3 values, unevenly held across 28 of 36 collectors). If your coverage map only has service/Region/resourceType columns, this page is unmappable and should be recorded as such rather than forced into the nearest column.

features.featureName: Amazon Inspector SBOM Generator comprehensive ecosystem collection — Supported ecosystems (the `extra-ecosystems` scanner group)
features.reasoning: The coverage claim the page actually supports is "the SBOM Generator collects application X". X is a named piece of third-party software — 7-Zip, Apache Struts, Jenkins, Redis, Microsoft Exchange Server, Cursor, Zed — which exists whether or not Amazon Inspector exists, so the axis is external, not a catalogue. That is the important call here: it is tempting to read this as Inspector publishing a list about itself, but the values are other vendors' products. The axis is the application, not the "Ecosystems" column: that column is a vendor/family grouping of wildly unequal size ("Microsoft applications" is one row holding 15 applications, "Nginx" is one row holding one), so counting 39 rows compares things that are not comparable. The 36 detail sections are organised by COLLECTOR, not by the table's vendor rows, so they do not map 1:1 onto the 39 rows — Anthropic's two products split across the "Claude Code" and "Standalone AI applications" sections; Jan, LM Studio, GPT4All and Tabby are four separate table rows served by one "Standalone AI applications" section; GitHub, Kiro, Anysphere, Codeium and Zed Industries are vendor rows whose sections are named after the product. The denominator — all software in the world — is unbounded, so this axis yields a supported-set, never a percentage.
features.scope: Two nested groupings, both stated by the page: (a) the summary table's "Ecosystems" column — 39 vendor/family rows — as the coarse grain over the same applications; (b) per-collector operating system, given in the 36 detail sections and captured as its own feature below. No per-Region and no per-scan-target dimension is enumerated.
features.statuses:
79 supported, 0 stated as not supported on this axis. There is no Yes/No column, no strikethrough, no retired/deprecated marking, and no negative row. Derivation of 79, counted by hand: the table's Applications cells split on
give 88 entries; subtract the 6 that are file extensions, not applications (the Generic AI/ML Models row: .gguf, .safetensors, .onnx, .pt, .pth, .h5) and the 3 that are WordPress component types (core, plugin, theme), leaving 79 application entries; subtract 1 for the duplicate (row 28 "Node" and row 29 "Node.JS" are the same node runtime, and only one detail section, "Node.JS runtime collection", exists) = 78 from the table; add Puppeteer, named as a supported application in the Google detail section but absent from the table = 79. The many negative-sounding sentences on this page are NOT axis exclusions and must not become not-covered rows: they are version floors and scope caveats — OpenSSL "Custom or forked OpenSSL variants and versions lower than 3.0.0 are not supported"; Google "puppeteer-core is not included"; HuggingFace "Models downloaded using `hf download --local-dir` are not currently supported"; GitHub Copilot "excludes the separate `github.copilot-chat-*` extension"; Docker "Vulnerability evaluation only applies to Docker versions 25.0.0+"; Elasticsearch "only applies to Elasticsearch version 7.17.0"; Apache httpd "version 2.0 and higher"; Jenkins "version 2.400.* and higher"; Microsoft applications "detections in the InspectorScan API are only supported for versions of these applications released in 2021 (or later)"; AI agent skills "Skills are not versioned"; Generic AI/ML Models "No PURL is generated for components detected by this collector". Each constrains a version range or an output field for an application that IS covered.

features.reasoning: Operating systems are a universe that exists independently of Amazon Inspector, so this is external and a real ratio (out of 3) is meaningful per collector. The page states this dimension deliberately and repeatedly under a "Supported platforms" heading, and the sets genuinely differ between collectors, which is what makes it coverage rather than boilerplate. The values are the OS headings themselves — Linux, macOS, Windows — not the install paths listed beneath them. The paths (`C:/Program Files/7-Zip/7z.exe`, `~/.nvm/versions/node/*/bin/node`) are detection mechanics and must not be mistaken for axis values.
features.scope: Per ecosystem collector. Of the 36 collector detail sections, 28 enumerate an explicit OS list, 1 (AI IDE extensions) says only "Cross-platform", and 7 state no platform at all (Java, HuggingFace, Google, Ollama Model Collector, OpenSSL, WordPress, Microsoft applications).
features.statuses: 3 values on the axis: Linux, macOS, Windows. AWS's wording is inconsistent and must be normalised — "Unix" appears as a heading for Apache httpd, and "Unix – Linux and macOS" for Curl and Libcurl; "Linux and macOS" is one heading covering two values; "Windows and Linux" appears in prose for Standalone AI applications. This is the ONLY axis on the page with genuine not-covered values, stated by omission of an OS heading: Windows-only (7-Zip, Microsoft SQL Server) — Linux and macOS not covered; Linux-only (Oracle Database Server, both Atlassian subsections) — macOS and Windows not covered; Linux+macOS, no Windows (Redis, Kiro CLI, Curl, Libcurl, Generic AI/ML Models); Linux+Windows, no macOS (Cursor, Windsurf, Zed, Apache Struts, Apache httpd, Standalone AI applications); all three (AI agent skills, Amazon Q Developer, Apache Cassandra, Apache tomcat, Claude Code, Conda, Docker binaries, Elasticsearch, GitHub Copilot, Jenkins, MariaDB, MySQL, MongoDB, Nginx, Node.JS runtime, Ollama, OpenSSH, PHP). Absence of a platform block in the other 8 sections is unknown, not "no" — do not record those as not-covered.

features.featureName: Generic AI/ML Models ecosystem collection — model file detection by file extension
features.reasoning: This is a different axis from every other row on the page. The other collectors answer "which application do you find?"; this one answers "which model file format do you recognise?". Model serialisation formats are an external universe defined by PyTorch, Keras, ONNX and llama.cpp, not by AWS. Keeping it separate matters: fold it into the application axis and six file extensions get typed as six applications, which is wrong on its face. Note .pt and .pth are two extensions for one framework (PyTorch), so the count is 6 extensions over 5 formats — count the extensions, since that is what the collector matches on.
features.scope: Linux and macOS only (no Windows heading). Detected files are emitted with the `machine-learning-model` component type and no PURL.
features.statuses: 6 supported, 0 not supported: .gguf (GGUF), .safetensors (Safetensors), .onnx (ONNX), .pt (PyTorch), .pth (PyTorch), .h5 (Keras / HDF5). Counted from both the table cell and the Key features bullet, which agree.

features.reasoning: The heading is "Supported components", not "Supported applications", and the values are WordPress's own extension taxonomy — a universe WordPress defines, not Amazon Inspector — so external. It is a genuinely enumerable and complete set (WordPress has exactly these three installable artifact classes), which makes it the one axis on this page where a ratio would actually be meaningful: 3 of 3.
features.scope: No operating system stated for this collector.
features.statuses: 3 supported, 0 not supported: WordPress core, WordPress plugins, WordPress themes. Stated under a "Supported components" heading (the table row says core / plugin / theme).

pageTitle: Amazon Inspector SBOM Generator comprehensive ecosystem collection
shouldNotExtract: Not coverage, do not extract: every "Example PURL" / "Sample PURL" block (pkg:generic/7zip/7zip@25.01 and roughly forty others) — these are output-format examples, and their vendor namespaces are not axis values. Every example file body: ap_release.h, curlver.h, opensslv.h, state.json, META-INF/MANIFEST.MF, chrome/VERSION, the puppeteer package.json, and especially the two long Java MODULES="java.base java.compiler ..." strings, which a naive splitter would happily turn into about seventy fake covered values. Installation paths, glob patterns, Windows registry keys (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\...), VS Code extension IDs (continue.continue-*, sourcegraph.cody-ai-*, saoudrizwan.claude-dev-*) and JetBrains plugin directories — detection mechanics, not values. Binary section names (.rodata, .rdata, __cstring). The "Key features" bullets, which describe HOW a version is parsed. Scanner names and CLI options: `extra-ecosystems`, `ai-ide-extensions`, `--additional-scanners`, `--path`, and the whole "Scanner name" and "Version source" columns of the Standalone AI applications table — those columns are implementation identifiers sitting inside an otherwise legitimate coverage table, so take only its "Application" column. Version floors and their prose (2021+, 25.0.0+, 7.2 and higher, 2.400.*, 3.0.0 and above) — they qualify a covered value, they are not values. CycloneDX component types (application, machine-learning-model) and PURL types (generic, huggingface, ollama). The <a name="w2aac39c27..."> anchors. The intro paragraph. The trailing "See also" bullet about AWS Agent Toolkit skills and `aws agent-toolkit search-skills` — that is the AI-coding-assistant boilerplate AWS now appends to every page and carries zero coverage signal. Outbound links to sbom-generator.html, pptr.dev and learn.microsoft.com.
trap:
A careless parser reads the summary table, counts 39 rows in the "Ecosystems" column, and reports "39 ecosystems, 39 supported, 100% coverage". Five things are wrong with that at once. (1) 39 is inflated: rows 28 "Node" and 29 "Node.JS" are the same node runtime listed twice — there is exactly one "Node.JS runtime collection" section serving both. (2) The Ecosystems column is a vendor grouping, not a comparable universe. "Microsoft applications" is one row holding 15 applications; "Nginx" is one row holding one. Counting rows treats those as equal. (3) Splitting the Applications cells on
yields 88 entries, but 6 of them are file extensions (.gguf, .safetensors, .onnx, .pt, .pth, .h5) and 3 are WordPress component types (core, plugin, theme). Typed as applications, they are simply false. (4) The table is not the whole page. The Google detail section names Puppeteer as a supported application; the table's Google row says only "Chrome". Trusting the table alone silently undercounts, and trusting only the 36 detail-section headings misses the vendor rows (Jan, LM Studio, GPT4All, TabbyML) that have no section of their own. (5) The percentage itself is meaningless. Every value on the page is supported by construction — there is no Yes/No column and no denominator — so 100% is a restatement of "this is a list", not a measurement. Two further specific errors. The parser sees a dozen sentences containing "not supported" / "not included" / "only applies to" and emits not-covered rows for OpenSSL, Puppeteer, HuggingFace, Docker and Elasticsearch — but every one of those is a VERSION FLOOR or an output caveat on an application that IS covered, not a value excluded from an axis. And it ignores the one axis on this page that carries real negatives: per-collector operating system, where 7-Zip and Microsoft SQL Server are Windows-only, Oracle Database Server and Atlassian are Linux-only, and Cursor, Windsurf and Zed have no macOS — genuine "does not reach" claims, stated by the silent omission of an OS heading rather than by any word a keyword search would find. It must also not infer "no" from the 7 sections that state no platform at all; that is unknown, not unsupported.
whatThePageStates: This page documents what the Amazon Inspector SBOM Generator (Sbomgen) can detect BEYOND OS package managers — third-party applications installed by other means (manual install, Electron bundles, static binaries, IDE extension directories, model caches). These collectors run under the `extra-ecosystems` scanner group, on by default for container and localhost scans, added with `--additional-scanners` for other scan types. It opens with one summary table of 39 "Ecosystems" rows against an "Applications" column, then 36 per-collector detail sections, each giving supported applications, how the version is extracted, and which operating systems' install paths are scanned. It is an allow-list page: it enumerates only what IS collected, with no Yes/No column and no denominator anywhere.
